sentences.text: Rhamphorhynchus is a genus of long-tailed pterosaurs from the Jurassic period, named for its beak and snout.
The smallest known specimen of this genus had a wingspan of only 290 mm.
In contrast, the largest known individual reached an estimated wingspan of 1.8 meters.
The genus Rhamphorhynchus was formally described by Hermann von Meyer in 1846.
It was originally named Ornithocephalus muensteri because scientists at the time incorrectly thought Ornithocephalus was the valid name for Pterodactylus.
The best-preserved specimens come from the Solnhofen limestone in Bavaria, Germany.
A new species, R. etchesi, was named in 2015 based on wing remains from the Kimmeridge Clay in the United Kingdom.
This newer species is distinguished from others by a unique length ratio between its first and second wing phalanges.
Fossil evidence from stomach contents and coprolites confirms that this animal ate fish and cephalopods.
The intermeshing teeth of the animal suggest a diet focused on fish.
Adults developed a strong upward hook at the tip of the lower jaw.
Recent evidence suggests the animal likely foraged while swimming, similar to modern aquatic birds.
Broad, large feet were useful for propulsion while swimming.
Comparisons of scleral rings suggest Rhamphorhynchus may have been nocturnal, similar to modern nocturnal seabirds.
A fossil specimen shows the jaws of a fish piercing the wing membrane of an individual.
A 2020 study supported the theory that the animal was precocial and could fly soon after hatching.
The type species of the genus is R. muensteri.
Phylogenetic analysis places R. muensteri in the family Rhamphorhynchidae, as a sister taxon to Cacibupteryx and Nesodactylus.
Rhamphorhynchus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically the Tithonian age.
The animal lived from the Oxfordian to the Tithonian stages, between 159 and 143.1 million years ago.
It is debated whether Rhamphorhynchus had a crest; while Ferdinand Broili reported one in 1927, later examinations found no evidence of it.
Bennett suggested Rhamphorhynchus likely had an ectothermic (cold-blooded) metabolism, though he noted more studies were needed to confirm this.
Bennett found that specimens grouped into small-headed and large-headed sets, but concluded the case for sexual dimorphism was inconclusive due to a lack of morphological differences.
